title: Advice to students, New York work and leaving for Louisville
summary: He tells students to go where the work is; as machines replaced players he left New York for teaching at Louisville.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Speaking of talent, the students that you’ve had when you were in academia, did you have any advice for them when they were about to graduate to help them enter the music world?

Not unless they really asked, but you know you could tell the sincerity of a student after working with them for a couple of years. And if they had, if they said, “I want to write music for a living” then I would give them the advice, you have to go where the food is, you have to go to Los Angeles or go to New York or go to London or Toronto, but you have to go where the writing is important and where there is a living to be made writing. Now today yes you can do everything from a distance. But you’re not going to get the work. You have to be out there schmoozing, you have to be visible. And a lot of clients, they don’t want to know that you’re a hundred miles away. They want to know that they can see you for lunch tomorrow and be there, and you know, those kinds of gigs. But I tell them, you go where the food is, and that’s where it is.
For you was that mostly New York and Los Angeles?

Yeah. Mostly New York. Yeah. And that was — of course that was a different period. You know we got paid to do jingle demos. You got paid for the demo, and then they would like it, approve it, and then you’d get the full band. But those were different days. But New York was definitely a fertile ground. Broadway. I shouldn’t make such a blanket statement but as far as the union is concerned the only thing for musicians today is Broadway.
Did you ever do demos that turned out to be the record?
Yeah. And a friend of mine, Jay Chattaway, he did an orchestra mock-up on synthesizers and they loved it and they used that instead of the full orchestra. It happens.
What were the other things that happened that you sensed as a, uh oh, this seems like a musical, a big change in the scene, and how am I going to deal with this.

That’s when I left New York State and moved down here to teach at the University of Louisville. Everything was going south. I mean machines were replacing humans, even the jingles, people were doing them for free just to get the airplay, get the ASCAP airplay. Same out in California. Kids were doing TV themes and still are for nothing just to get the exposure and get the ASCAP, you know, or BMI airplay, performance royalties. So that’s when I knew that it was time, it was definitely time. And they came after me so I says what the heck, why not.

Yes. That’s right, with two kids, health insurance. Plus I enjoyed teaching. I really enjoy teaching, and especially at the college level ‘cause you’ve got a certain caliber of student that you can just jump in here and really bring them up. Yeah. I really enjoyed the teaching.
